propositions.text: Applicant seeks judicial review of visa officer's refusal of permanent residence application under Convention refugee abroad class.
propositions.quote: The Applicant, Sadia Ahmed Osman, seeks judicial review of a decision of the visa officer at the Canadian High Commission in Nairobi, Kenya, dated August 29, 2019, refusing her application for permanent residence as part of the Convention refugee abroad class on the grounds that she did not answer truthfully the questions in her application and those put to her during her examination, contrary to the provisions of subsections 11(1) and 16(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [Act].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant seeks judicial review of a visa officer's refusal of her permanent residence application for untruthfulness under the Act.

propositions.text: Applicant admits lying on application but argues policy in section 22 of Regulations should forgive breaches of subsection 16(1) of the Act.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman admitted in her response to a procedural fairness letter that she indeed lied on her application as to whether she had ever been issued a passport and whether she had in the past ever used another name or applied for a visa, however, she argues that she should be forgiven for her transgressions on account of the policy imperative inherent in section 22 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227 [Regulations].

propositions.text: Applicant argues subsection 16(1) should be read with section 22 exempting refugee claimants from inadmissibility for misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman argues that because she is applying under the Convention refugee abroad class, subsection 16(1) of the Act – the obligation to answer truthfully – should be read in conjunction with section 22 of the Regulations, which exempts refugee claimants from the application of paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act – inadmissibility for misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Applicant proposes policy in section 22 should shield her from consequences of breaching subsection 16(1) in permanent residence application context.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman proposes that the same policy imperative upon which section 22 of the Regulations is premised should also shield her from the consequences of breaching subsection 16(1) of the Act in the context of an application for a permanent residence visa under the Convention refugee abroad class.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant admits lying but argues section 22 policy should forgive breaches of subsection 16(1) in refugee abroad class applications.

propositions.text: Court dismisses application, stating judicial amendment to Act is not possible.
propositions.quote: I am dismissing Ms. Osman’s application. Although the issue raised by Ms. Osman may well justify a review by the Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship [Minister], however, what Ms. Osman is seeking, in short, is a judicial amendment to the Act, something I cannot do.

propositions.text: If Parliament intended to extend section 22 policy to subsection 16(1) breaches, it would have done so.
propositions.quote: If Parliament intended to extend the policy imperative supporting section 22 of the Regulations to forgive breaches of subsection 16(1) of the Act in this context, it would have done so.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application, saying judicial amendment to extend section 22 policy to subsection 16(1) breaches is not possible.

propositions.text: Applicant is 36-year-old Somali woman, co-owner of a restaurant in Mogadishu.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman is a 36-year-old woman who was born in Somalia. She was the co-owner, along with her uncle and aunt, of a restaurant in the city of Mogadishu.

propositions.text: In 2013, Al-Shabab men demanded applicant marry one of them; she refused; her uncle and aunt were assassinated.
propositions.quote: On December 5, 2013, five men entered the restaurant and demanded that Ms. Osman marry one of them; she refused. The men were members of Al-Shabab and Ms. Osman’s refusal had consequences: Ms. Osman’s uncle and aunt were assassinated by the Al-Shabab members, who returned to the restaurant looking for Ms. Osman, after her uncle refused to reveal where she was.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant is a 36-year-old Somali woman whose relatives were assassinated by Al-Shabab after she refused forced marriage.

propositions.text: Applicant applied for refugee protection in Thailand in 2015 under Private Sponsorship of Refugees Program for herself and dependants.
propositions.quote: On October 19, 2015, while in Thailand, Ms. Osman submitted an application for refugee protection under the Private Sponsorship of Refugees Program, sponsored by the Diocese of Rupert’s Land, for herself and for her dependants – the children of her deceased uncle and aunt who were living in Somalia at the time and who Ms. Osman undertook to care for following the death of their parents.

propositions.text: Children's applications were disassociated in December 2015 as they were 'ineligible family members' not living with applicant.
propositions.quote: The children’s applications were disassociated from that of Ms. Osman in December 2015 because the children were considered “ineligible family members” on account of the fact that they were not living together with Ms. Osman.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant applied for refugee protection in Thailand in 2015; children's applications were disassociated as ineligible family members.

propositions.text: Applicant declared never used other names, never applied for or refused refugee protection or visa, and never issued a passport.
propositions.quote: In her application, Ms. Osman declared that she had never used any other name other than her own. Moreover, during her interview with an immigration officer in October 2018 in Ethiopia – Ms. Osman had been deported from Thailand two months earlier – Ms. Osman stated that she had never applied for or been refused refugee protection or applied for a visa to Canada or any another country. She also declared that she had never been issued a passport.

paragraphs.summary: The court states applicant declared never using other names, applying for visas, or having a passport.

propositions.text: Biometric tracing linked applicant to 2015 U.S. visa application under different name and birthdate in Malaysia.
propositions.quote: Biometric tracing – information sharing with the United States – revealed that Ms. Osman’s biometrics were associated with a 2015 U.S. visa application originating from Malaysia made by Ms. Osman under a different name and with a different date of birth.

propositions.text: Applicant traveled to Malaysia under false identity, used same false name for U.S. visa, and obtained Somali passport under alias.
propositions.quote: It would seem that Ms. Osman had travelled to Malaysia under a false identity prior to travelling to Thailand and Ethiopia and had used that same false name to apply for a U.S. visa while she was there. She had also obtained a Somali passport under that alias.

paragraphs.summary: The court states biometric tracing linked applicant to a 2015 U.S. visa application under a false identity and alias passport.

propositions.text: Visa officer sent procedural fairness letter raising concerns about applicant's untruthfulness regarding identity and visa history.
propositions.quote: On June 5, 2019, a visa officer sent a procedural fairness letter to Ms. Osman giving her the opportunity to address the visa officer’s concerns: In your application, you have stated that Sadia Ahmed Osman has never been known by any other name; that she had never applied for or been refused a visa to any country; and that she had never been issued a passport. However, this office has received information that Sadia Ahmed Osman used a Somali passport under the name of Fardowso Ahmed Hussein to apply for a US visa in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia on January 29, 2015. I am therefore concerned that you have not been truthful regarding your identity; whether you have been known by another name; whether you have applied for or been refused a visa to any country, and if you have been issued a passport in the past. Before a decision is made in your case, I am providing you with the opportunity to comment on the above concerns or provide any documents or explanation in writing.

paragraphs.summary: The visa officer sent a procedural fairness letter raising concerns about applicant's untruthfulness on identity and visa history.

propositions.text: Visa officer's concerns included untruthfulness and identity issues affecting admissibility screening.
propositions.quote: It would seem that the visa officer’s concerns went beyond the truthfulness in and of itself of Ms. Osman’s responses; the Global Case Management System [GCMS] notes indicate that the visa officer also had concerns regarding her identity: [March 4, 2019] I have reviewed the US info sharing. Sadia’s name and biographic details do not return a hit however her biometrics do. Her biometrics demonstrate that she applied for a US visa while in Malaysia in 2015 under a different name and DOB. On her forms, Sadia declared that she had no other names and had never been known by any other names. During interview, she testified that she had never applied for or been refused a visa to any country other than being smuggled to Malaysia. During interview, she testified that she had never been issued a passport however US info sharing shows that she was in possession of a Somali passport. This applicant has not been truthful or honest regarding her age or identity. She has not been honest regarding her history. This information is necessary to assess her identity and to ensure that proper admissibility screening can be done. To await results from UNHCR verification so that if issues [with that] document, applicant can be confronted [with] everything at once. [Emphasis added.]

paragraphs.summary: Visa officer's notes show concerns about applicant's untruthfulness and identity affecting admissibility screening.

propositions.text: Applicant explained using false name to escape persecution and protect life, believing she was not misrepresenting material fact.
propositions.quote: In a letter dated June 10, 2019, Ms. Osman responded to the procedural fairness letter and acknowledged that she used the name of Fardowso Ahmed Hussein to apply for a U.S. visa, with the following explanation: . . . I would like to provide my honest explanations to the best of my ability. This is the first time I feel secure to disclose the truth and the whole truth to your respected office who has given me the opportunity to explain the reasons behind using different names including my relatives in Canada. . . . In a desperate attempt to save our lives I and my family were living in disguised while trying to seek protection from place to place because I had lost many relatives and family members to the horrible crimes committed by AL SHABAB and their supporters. Since then I have been leaving [sic] in fear all my life to the present time. Because of fearful life surrounding me and my family I took a desperate step to hide my real identity to avoid being a target and in attempt to lead a normal life in the community as I have witnessed a gross violation of human right abuse and barbaric actions taken against many innocent human beings even after I escaped serious persecutions at home land. While in search of protection being displaced inside the country and trying to save my life I was advised many times to avoid using my real identity. And the name Fardowso Ahmed Hussein was the name that I was given by a broker who advised me to use his diseased sister’s name so that I can be able to flee from Somalia. Together with other community members I have applied using this name for the visa lottery program to USA in 2015 in search of protection and to live a peaceful life. Because my life was at risk I honestly and reasonably believed I was not misrepresenting a material fact. I am still having that fear until now, and scares [sic] for my life in my day to day survival as refugee because there is always risk of being targeted by individuals and groups who are associated with AL SHABAB, informants and their sympathizers. . . . [Emphasis added.]

paragraphs.summary: Applicant explained using false name to escape persecution, believing she was not misrepresenting material facts.

propositions.text: Visa officer refused application citing subsection 16(1) for untruthfulness about identity and visa history.
propositions.quote: On August 29, 2019, the visa officer refused Ms. Osman’s application for a visa as a permanent resident [the refusal decision] because she did not meet the requirements of the Act: Ms. Osman was found to have been untruthful in her application. Citing subsection 16(1) of the Act, the visa officer stated: In your application, you have stated that Sadia Ahmed Osman has never been known by any other name; that she had never applied for or been refused a visa to any country; and that she had never been issued a passport. However, this office has received information that Sadia Ahmed Osman used a Somali passport under the name of Fardowso Ahmed Hussein to apply for a US visa in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia on January 29, 2015. I am therefore not satisfied that you have been truthful regarding Sadia Ahmed Osman’s identity; whether she has been known by another name; whether she has applied for or been refused a visa to any country; and if she has been issued a passport in the past. [Emphasis added.]

paragraphs.summary: Visa officer refused applicant's permanent resident visa citing subsection 16(1) for untruthfulness about identity and visa history.

propositions.text: Visa officer refused application under subsection 11(1) without addressing applicant's explanation for lying.
propositions.quote: The visa officer refused Ms. Osman’s application pursuant to subsection 11(1) of the Act. The refusal decision did not refer to Ms. Osman’s reply to the procedural fairness letter, nor did it address her explanation as to why she lied.

propositions.text: Visa officer's notes show concern that untruthfulness affected identity establishment and admissibility screening.
propositions.quote: As stated earlier, the GCMS notes of the visa officer reflect a concern not only with respect to the truthfulness of Ms. Osman’s answers, but also more particularly with respect to the fact that such untruthfulness affected the establishment of her identity: [August 29, 2019] Application reviewed this day. Info-sharing shows the [sic] Sadia Ahmed Osman applied for a US visa with a Somalia passport under the name of Fardowso Ahmed Hussein in Malaysia. She had stated in her present application that she had no other names, had never been known by any other names, that she had never applied for or been refused a visa to any country, and that she had never been issued a passport. A16 and identity concerns sent in PFL. PFL response received confirming that the applicant had a false name and passport. I have reviewed the response in detail. After having reviewed the response, I am not satisfied that the applicant has met the requirements of the act. [Emphasis added.]

paragraphs.summary: Visa officer refused application under subsection 11(1) without addressing applicant's explanation; untruthfulness affected identity establishment.

propositions.text: Applicant filed application for leave and judicial review on September 17, 2020; leave granted with extension of time.
propositions.quote: On September 17, 2020, Ms. Osman filed her application for leave and judicial review of the refusal decision. Leave was granted by this Court along with an extension of time.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant filed for judicial review; leave granted with extension of time.

propositions.text: Sole issue is whether refusal decision is reasonable; parties agree standard of review is reasonableness.
propositions.quote: The sole issue in the present application is whether the refusal decision is reasonable. The parties agree that the applicable standard of review under the circumstances is reasonableness.

propositions.text: Court set out applicable statutory and regulatory provisions in annex to decision.
propositions.quote: I should also mention that I have set out the applicable statutory and regulatory provisions in the annex to my decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the sole issue is reasonableness of refusal; parties agree on standard; court annexed provisions.

propositions.text: Court will address each of applicant's arguments separately; applicant cites no case law except on standard of review.
propositions.quote: I will deal with each of Ms. Osman’s arguments separately. I should mention that Ms. Osman cites no case law in support for her assertions other than on the issue of the standard of review.

paragraphs.summary: Court will address applicant's arguments separately; applicant cites no case law except on standard of review.

propositions.text: Subsection 11(1) requires visa officer to be satisfied applicant is not inadmissible and meets Act requirements before issuing visa.
propositions.quote: Subsection 11(1) of the Act provides that a visa officer may issue a visa to a foreign national if, following an examination, the officer is satisfied that the foreign national is not inadmissible and meets the requirements of the Act. Both conditions must be met before a visa officer exercises his or her discretion in respect of the issuance of a visa.

paragraphs.summary: Court states subsection 11(1) requires visa officer to be satisfied applicant is not inadmissible and meets Act requirements before issuing visa.

propositions.text: Paragraph 40(1)(a) provides inadmissibility for misrepresentation; section 22 suspends its application for pending refugee claimants.
propositions.quote: One of the grounds of inadmissibility is misrepresentation in relation to material facts in relation to a relevant matter that induces or could induce an error in the administration of the Act (paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act). However, the application of paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act is suspended in the case of individuals who have claimed refugee protection where the disposition of their claim is pending (section 22 of the Regulations).

propositions.text: Applicants must answer truthfully all questions for examination (subsection 16(1) of the Act).
propositions.quote: In addition, one of the requirements of the Act is for applicants for a visa to enter Canada to answer truthfully all questions put to them for the purpose of their examination (subsection 16(1) of the Act).

paragraphs.summary: Court states inadmissibility for misrepresentation is suspended for pending refugee claimants; applicants must answer truthfully under subsection 16(1).

propositions.text: Subsection 16(1) and paragraph 40(1)(a) both deal with failure to be forthright in representations.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman focuses on the interplay between paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act and section 22 of the Regulations on the one hand and subsection 16(1) of the Act on the other hand. I accept that both subsection 16(1) and paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act are similar in that they both deal with the failure of an applicant to be forthright in his or her representations.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds subsection 16(1) and paragraph 40(1)(a) both address failure to be forthright in representations.

propositions.text: Applicant argues no substantial difference between 'misrepresentation' and 'untruthfulness'; refusal was based on misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman argues that there is no substantial difference between a “misrepresentation” and “untruthfulness” and that although the refusal decision does not refer to paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act, in substance, the refusal was based on a finding of misrepresentation.

propositions.text: Applicant argues she should be exempted from paragraph 40(1)(a) application under section 22 as Convention refugee abroad class applicant.
propositions.quote: Consequently, and even though her application was routed through the visa office, she was nonetheless applying for a visa under the Convention refugee abroad class and should have been exempted from the application of paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act pursuant to section 22 of the Regulations.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues misrepresentation and untruthfulness are similar and she should be exempted from inadmissibility under section 22.

propositions.text: Policy in section 22 recognizes refugees may lie to escape persecution; denying protection for misrepresentation frustrates refugee legislation.
propositions.quote: The policy imperative underpinning section 22 of the Regulations is that in terms of refugee protection, the legislation recognizes that people must sometimes lie to escape persecution and that it would frustrate the very purpose of refugee legislation if one says that the means of escape becomes justification for denying protection.

propositions.text: Applicant submits Act must be read as whole; policy prohibiting denial for misrepresentation must apply regardless of process used.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman submits that the Act must be read as a whole and not at cross-purposes with itself, and that the policy imperative which prohibits the denial of refugee protection for reasons of misrepresentation must apply regardless of the process undertaken by the applicant to seek such protection;

propositions.text: Applicant argues paragraph 40(1)(a) and section 22 cannot be ignored when applying subsection 16(1) as that would defeat section 22's purpose and allow indirect denial.
propositions.quote: she argues that paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act and section 22 of the Regulations cannot be ignored when applying subsection 16(1) in this context as to do so would defeat the purpose and the policy underpinning of section 22 of the Regulations and thus allow a visa officer to do indirectly what he or she cannot do directly.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues policy in section 22 protects refugees who lie; Act must be read as whole; subsection 16(1) must not defeat section 22's purpose.

propositions.text: Section 22's intent is reflected in UNHCR Handbook paragraphs 198-199, emphasizing fear of authorities and need to evaluate untrue statements contextually.
propositions.quote: The intent of section 22 of the Regulations, argues Ms. Osman, is reflected in paragraphs 198 and 199 of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees’ Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status (Reissued – Geneva, February 2019), which state: 198. A person who, because of his experiences, was in fear of the authorities in his own country may still feel apprehensive vis‑à‑vis any authority. He may therefore be afraid to speak freely and give a full and accurate account of his case. 199. While an initial interview should normally suffice to bring an applicant’s story to light, it may be necessary for the examiner to clarify any apparent inconsistencies and to resolve any contradictions in a further interview, and to find an explanation for any misrepresentation or concealment of material facts. Untrue statements by themselves are not a reason for refusal of refugee status and it is the examiner’s responsibility to evaluate such statements in the light of all the circumstances of the case. [Emphasis added.]

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues section 22's intent aligns with UNHCR Handbook emphasizing fear of authorities and context in evaluating untrue statements.

propositions.text: If Ms. Osman had made an inland refugee claim, subsection 16(1) would not apply until permanent residence application, avoiding removal risk.
propositions.quote: Had she arrived in Canada and made an inland claim for refugee protection, her claim would have been referred to the Refugee Protection Division and assessed accordingly, during which time subsection 16(1) of the Act would not apply as she would not be applying for a visa.

propositions.text: Applying under Convention refugee abroad class subjects application to subsections 11(1) and 16(1) before refugee claim assessment.
propositions.quote: by applying under the Convention refugee abroad class, her application for permanent residence must pass through the visa office, which subjects her application to the requirements of subsections 11(1) and 16(1) of the Act prior to having her claim for refugee protection assessed.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues inland claims avoid subsection 16(1) until permanent residence, but Convention refugee abroad class subjects application to subsections 11(1) and 16(1) first.

propositions.text: Distinction in Act's application conflicts with policy and objectives, allowing visa officers to deny refugee protection improperly.
propositions.quote: Such a distinction in the application of the underlying principles of the Act, says Ms. Osman, cannot stand in light of the policy imperative underlying section 22 of the Regulations and the objectives of the Act set out in section 3

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues the distinction conflicts with policy and Act objectives, enabling improper visa refusals.

propositions.text: Subsection 16(1) and paragraph 40(1)(a) differ; paragraph 40(1)(a) requires materiality and relevance and causes inadmissibility, unlike subsection 16(1).
propositions.quote: subsection 16(1) and paragraph 40(1)(a) are separate provisions with different applications and consequences; the application of paragraph 40(1)(a) requires the elements of materiality and relevance and brings with it the stigma of being inadmissible to Canada for five years

propositions.text: A refugee claimant may be excused for misrepresentation under inland claim but barred under Convention refugee abroad class for untruthfulness not material or relevant.
propositions.quote: a refugee claimant in an inland claim may be excused for making a misrepresentation regarding a material fact relating to a relevant matter, but the same claimant making the same claim under the Convention refugee abroad class may be barred for untruthfulness that is neither material nor relates to a relevant matter

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues subsection 16(1) is broader than paragraph 40(1)(a), causing inconsistent treatment of refugee claimants.

propositions.text: Section 109 requires materiality, relevance, and no other evidence to vacate refugee protection, unlike subsection 16(1) denial conditions.
propositions.quote: for refugee protection to be vacated, three conditions must be met: the misrepresentation must be material, the misrepresentation must relate to a relevant matter, and there must be no other sufficient evidence to justify refugee protection

propositions.text: Subsection 16(1) denial of refugee protection does not require these conditions.
propositions.quote: None of those conditions need be met so as to deny refugee protection for reasons set out in subsection 16(1) of the Act.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues section 109 conditions to vacate refugee protection differ from subsection 16(1) denial conditions.

propositions.text: Subsection 16(1) must be interpreted with Act's objectives and policies to avoid internal inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: the obligation of truthfulness set out in subsection 16(1) of the Act be interpreted in a way as to avoid internal inconsistencies in the Act; subsection 16(1) cannot be viewed in isolation and must be looked at along with the objectives and policies of the Act

propositions.text: Refugee protection principles should not be sacrificed for truthfulness obligations.
propositions.quote: the principles underlying refugee protection should not be sacrificed at the altar of truthfulness.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues subsection 16(1) must be interpreted with Act's objectives to avoid conflict and protect refugee principles.

propositions.text: Minister argues Act provisions are clear and Ms. Osman's argument was dismissed in Lhamo case.
propositions.quote: The Minister argues that there is no room in this case for statutory interpretation as the provisions of the Act are clear and unambiguous and, in any event, suggests that the argument being raised by Ms. Osman has already been dealt with and dismissed by this Court in Lhamo v Canada

propositions.text: Court disagrees, finding Lhamo is a family reunification case and not helpful to Minister's argument.
propositions.quote: I disagree; the decision in Lhamo is a family reunification case and is of no assistance to the Minister.

paragraphs.summary: Minister argues Act is clear and Lhamo dismisses applicant's argument; court disagrees, finding Lhamo irrelevant.

propositions.text: Lhamo found visa applicants can be refused for untruthfulness under subsection 16(1) even if not inadmissible under subsection 21(2).
propositions.quote: Madam Justice Kane found that an applicant for a visa could indeed be refused a visa for this reason, and she stated the following: Although a person may not be inadmissible pursuant to the specific grounds of inadmissibility set out in subsection 21(3) [sic], they are not automatically admissible and provided with a visa. The requirements of the Act must be met. One of those requirements is that an applicant be truthful.

paragraphs.summary: Lhamo found visa applicants can be refused for untruthfulness under subsection 16(1) even if not inadmissible under subsection 21(2).

propositions.text: Ms. Osman's refugee claim is undetermined and subsection 40(1) inadmissibility cannot be invoked due to section 22 of Regulations.
propositions.quote: not only has Ms. Osman’s refugee claim not yet been determined, but unlike the situation in Lhamo, the very ground for inadmissibility that relates to her situation – misrepresentation under subsection 40(1) of the Act – cannot be invoked against her in relation to her refugee claim on account of section 22 of the Regulations.

propositions.text: Lhamo involved family members of determined Convention refugees subject to subsection 21(2) inadmissibility, unlike Ms. Osman's case.
propositions.quote: In Lhamo, the grounds of inadmissibility in question were specifically applicable, pursuant to subsection 21(2) of the Act, to family members of a claimant who had already been determined to be a Convention refugee.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Ms. Osman's claim undetermined and subsection 40(1) inadmissibility inapplicable, unlike Lhamo's family member case.

propositions.text: Court appreciates Ms. Osman's situation but disagrees with her position.
propositions.quote: I cannot agree with her position.

paragraphs.summary: Court disagrees with Ms. Osman's position despite understanding her situation.

propositions.text: Section 22 relieves refugee claimants from subsection 40(1) consequences but not subsection 16(1).
propositions.quote: section 22 of the Regulations relieves refugee claimants from the consequences of subsection 40(1) and not of subsection 16(1) of the Act.

propositions.text: Court will not unravel policy considerations when statutory provisions are clear and unambiguous.
propositions.quote: although context is important in statutory analysis, it is not for the Court to try to wade through all of the policy considerations to unravel why certain legislative schemes apply as they do in cases where the statutory provisions are clear and unambiguous.

propositions.text: Parliament could have shielded refugee claimants from subsection 16(1) consequences but chose not to and used different terms for lying in subsections 40(1) and 16(1).
propositions.quote: If Parliament intended to shield refugee claimants from the consequences of breaching subsection 16(1) where the vehicle used to seek refugee protection requires them to apply for permanent residency from abroad, it could easily have done so. Not only has it chosen not to, but it has in fact used different terms to identify what is commonly referred to as lying –the term “misrepresentation” is used in subsection 40(1) and the term “truthfulness” is used in subsection 16(1) of the Act

paragraphs.summary: Court finds section 22 shields from subsection 40(1) but not 16(1); Parliament chose different terms and did not shield claimants from 16(1).

propositions.text: Court sees no reason to interpret the Act as applicant requests.
propositions.quote: I see no reason to undertake the exercise of statutory interpretation being sought by Ms. Osman in this matter.

paragraphs.summary: Court refuses to interpret the Act as applicant requests.

propositions.text: Visa officer could have avoided subsection 16(1) and applied subsection 40(1) principles instead.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman argues that the visa officer could have avoided the application of subsection 16(1) of the Act and applied the principles applicable to subsection 40(1) of the Act in dealing with her situation.

propositions.text: Minister concedes visa officer could have used refugee claim procedure and discretion to avoid subsection 16(1).
propositions.quote: The Minister concedes that it was open to the visa officer to engage the refugee claim determination procedure and convene an interview of Ms. Osman ... and to exercise her/his discretion in not applying subsection 16(1) of the Act.

propositions.text: Issue is whether visa officer was obligated to avoid subsection 16(1); court finds no obligation and no unreasonableness in applying subsection 16(1).
propositions.quote: the issue here is not whether the visa officer could have proceeded in this way, but whether the visa officer was obligated to so proceed. I cannot see that where the visa officer was so obliged, and therefore, I do not see anything unreasonable in the visa officer’s application of subsection 16(1) of the Act under these circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues visa officer could avoid subsection 16(1); Minister concedes discretion; court finds no obligation or unreasonableness in applying subsection 16(1).

propositions.text: Visa officer refused application due to failure to be truthful under subsection 16(1); decision is not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The visa officer was not satisfied that Ms. Osman had met the requirement of the Act to be truthful pursuant to subsection 16(1) of the Act and therefore refused her application. I see nothing unreasonable with such a decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds visa officer's refusal for untruthfulness under subsection 16(1) reasonable.

propositions.text: Individuals deserve greater procedural protection when decisions have significant personal impact or harm.
propositions.quote: individuals are entitled to greater procedural protection when the decision in question involves the potential for significant personal impact or harm

paragraphs.summary: Prior authority states individuals deserve greater procedural protection for decisions with significant personal impact.

propositions.text: Visa officer should have acknowledged applicant's procedural fairness response and addressed reasons for untruthfulness in refusal decision.
propositions.quote: it was incumbent upon the visa officer to acknowledge her answer to the procedural fairness letter in the refusal decision, and to address the reasons provided by Ms. Osman on why she was untruthful on her application.

propositions.text: Applicant frames issue as procedural fairness, but court says it concerns reasonableness of decision and review approach.
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman frames the issue as one of procedural fairness, but it is not; any shortcomings in the reasons goes to the reasonableness of the decision and the issue of how a court is to conduct its reasonableness review.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues refusal decision lacked procedural fairness; court says issue is reasonableness of decision and review.

propositions.text: Refusal decision gave impression applicant's explanation was ignored, making procedural fairness letter insincere and refusal lacking responsive justification.
propositions.quote: the visa officer gave the impression that her attempt at explaining her actions was not even taken into consideration ... the refusal decision therefore fell short of the required level of responsive justification outlined by the Supreme Court in Vavilov

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues refusal decision ignored her explanation, lacking procedural fairness and justification.

propositions.text: GCMS notes confirm visa officer considered applicant's procedural fairness response; refusal reason was failure to be truthful.
propositions.quote: The GCMS notes confirm that the visa officer considered her answer to the procedural fairness letter. Once the visa officer identified the reason for the refusal ... there was no reason for the visa officer to also address the reasons given by Ms. Osman to explain her actions.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds visa officer considered applicant's response and refusal reason was failure to be truthful.

propositions.text: Refugee claims require heightened justification; decision-makers must justify consequences in light of facts and law (Vavilov).
propositions.quote: administrative decision-makers must “ensure that their reasons demonstrate that they have considered the consequences of a decision and that those consequences are justified in light of the facts and law” (Vavilov at paras 133 and 135).

propositions.text: Unlike Mohammad, visa officer reviewed and considered applicant's explanation but found it insufficient to avoid subsection 16(1) breach finding.
propositions.quote: Here, the GCMS notes confirm that the visa officer did review and consider Ms. Osman’s explanation, however, clearly decided that her explanation ... was not enough to avoid a finding that she contravened subsection 16(1) of the Act.

propositions.text: Refusal decision had harsh consequences but was reasonably made by visa officer.
propositions.quote: The refusal letter was admittedly a decision with harsh consequences, but I have not been persuaded that it was not open to the visa officer to reasonably make that determination.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds visa officer reasonably considered applicant's explanation and justified harsh refusal decision.

propositions.text: Omission of acknowledgement of applicant's response in refusal decision, instead in GCMS notes, does not make decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the omission of such an acknowledgement and statement in the refusal decision rather than in the GCMS notes does not render the refusal decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: Acknowledgement in refusal decision would be preferable but is not required for reasonableness.
propositions.quote: although an acknowledgement in the refusal decision of receipt of Ms. Osman’s answer ... may have been preferable under the circumstances

paragraphs.summary: Court finds omission of acknowledgement in refusal decision not unreasonable though preferable.

propositions.text: If visa officer applied paragraph 40(1)(a), any misrepresentation related to identity assessment and was not material to fear of persecution assessment
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman further argues that if the visa officer indeed intended to indirectly apply paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act, any misrepresentation on her part went to the assessment of her identity – the visa officer required clarity on identity “to ensure that proper admissibility screening can be done” – and was therefore not material to the assessment of her well-founded fear of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues misrepresentation related to identity was not material to fear of persecution assessment if paragraph 40(1)(a) applied.

propositions.text: Visa officer did not intend to apply paragraph 40(1)(a), so materiality concept does not apply
propositions.quote: Nothing suggests that the visa officer intended to apply paragraph 40(1)(a). Therefore, the concept of materiality is not applicable in this case.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds visa officer did not intend to apply paragraph 40(1)(a), so materiality is not applicable.

propositions.text: Dismiss Ms. Osman's application as visa officer's refusal was not unreasonable
propositions.quote: I would therefore dismiss Ms. Osman’s application as I find nothing unreasonable in the visa officer’s refusal decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses Ms. Osman's application finding visa officer's refusal reasonable.

propositions.text: Proposes certification of questions about legal permissibility of visa office finding inadmissibility without regard to application basis and duty of fairness in refusal letter
propositions.quote: Ms. Osman proposes that the following questions be certified pursuant to paragraph 74(d) of the Act: In light of sections 40(1)(a) and Regulation 22 the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, is it legally permissible for a visa office to find an applicant for permanent residence in Canada as a member of the Convention refugee abroad and the humanitarian protected persons abroad class inadmissible under section 16(1) of the Act without regard to the basis of the underlying application for membership in the class? Is the duty of fairness owed to an applicant for permanent residence in Canada as a member of the Convention refugee abroad and the humanitarian protected persons abroad class breached when the refusal letter replicates the personal fairness letter without acknowledgment of the response of the applicant to the personal fairness letter or an answer to the substance of that response?

paragraphs.summary: Applicant proposes certification of questions on visa office's legal permissibility and duty of fairness in refusal letter.

propositions.text: Both parties agree issue not raised before; court not persuaded applicant met certification test from Zhang
propositions.quote: Both parties acknowledge that this specific issue has not been raised before the Court in the past. In any event, I am not persuaded that Ms. Osman has met the test for certifying a question set out in Zhang v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FCA 168.

propositions.text: Paragraph 40(1)(a) and section 22 do not interact with subsection 16(1); amendment to Act needed for that
propositions.quote: Despite the very well argued case by counsel, the questions lack the hallmark of seriousness; put simply, paragraph 40(1)(a) of the Act and section 22 of the Regulations do not interact with subsection 16(1) of the Act. To do so would require an amendment to the Act.

propositions.text: Proposed questions lack broad significance or general importance; court declines to certify them
propositions.quote: Consequently, the proposed questions do not contemplate issues of broad significance or general importance, and I decline to certify the questions submitted.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds issue not raised before, questions lack seriousness and broad importance, and declines certification.

propositions.text: Dismiss application for judicial review with no questions certified
propositions.quote: The present application for judicial review is dismissed with no question to be certified.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application and declines to certify questions.
